items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we are given a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:
[MATH: x_{1} + 3x_{2} − x_{3} = 0; 2x_{1} − x_{2} + 4x_{3} = − 2; 5x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} = 1]

Content:
We can apply some operations to the augmented matrix that do not change the set of solutions for the corresponding system. These operations are called elementary row operations.

Content:
After applying an elementary row operation to the augmented matrix, the new corresponding system will have the same solutions.

Content:
There are three types of elementary row operations:

Content:
- switching any two rows:
[MATH: R_i \leftrightarrow R_j]
- multiplying (each element of) a row by a non-zero number:
[MATH: R_i := k R_i,\qquad k \neq 0]
- adding a multiple of one row to another row:
[MATH: R_j := R_j+k R_i,\qquad j \neq i]

Content:
In the notations above, the "[MATH: :=]" symbol is called the assignment operator. We use this to assign new values to every element of a given row.

Content:
For example, the row operation [MATH: R_1 := 2 R_1] means, "create a new row [MATH: 1] by taking the old row [MATH: 1] and multiplying it by [MATH: 2.]" When we do this, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: M|∼[1|3|− 1|0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]R_{1}:=2R_{1}; ∼[2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 3|2 ⋅ (− 1)|2 ⋅ 0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]; ∼[2|6|− 2|0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]]

Content:
A few final points on notation.

Content:
- We use the similarity symbol ([MATH: \sim]) to indicate when one matrix is transformed into another matrix using elementary row operations.
- The assignment operator [MATH: :=] is sometimes called the "walrus operator" because it looks like a walrus on its side!

sections.normalized_html: Which elementary row operation could transform the matrix [MATH: A] into the matrix [MATH: B], where [MATH: [− 4|− 2|4; 4|1|2; 1|2|3]]
sections.readable_text:
Which elementary row operation could transform the matrix [MATH: A] into the matrix [MATH: B], where
[MATH: [− 4|− 2|4; 4|1|2; 1|2|3]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the [MATH: 1]st and the [MATH: 3]rd rows are the same in both matrices. The only row that has been changed is the [MATH: 2]nd row.

Now, applying the operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2+1 \cdot R_1,] we get the following:

[MATH: A|= [− 4|− 2|4; 4|1|2; 1|2|3]R_{2}:=R_{2} + 1 ⋅ R_{1}; ∼[− 4|− 2|4; 4 + 1 ⋅ (− 4)|1 + 1 ⋅ (− 2)|2 + 1 ⋅ 4; 1|2|3]; ∼[− 4|− 2|4; 0|− 1|6; 1|2|3]; = B]

Therefore, the transformation could be done by the operation

[MATH: R_2:=R_2+1\cdot R_1]

or simply

[MATH: R_2:=R_2+R_1.]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: [3|1|− 2; − 1|5|6; 0|2|4]] which elementary row operation could make [MATH: a_{22}=0?]
sections.readable_text:
Given that
[MATH: [3|1|− 2; − 1|5|6; 0|2|4]] which elementary row operation could make [MATH: a_{22}=0?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In the given matrix, we have [MATH: a_{22}=5] and we want to perform an elementary row operation that makes [MATH: a_{22}=0.]

  • We cannot make [MATH: a_{22}=0] by switching two rows, because there are no rows with [MATH: 0] as the second entry.

  • We cannot multiply the second row by [MATH: 0,] because we are only allowed to multiply rows by nonzero constants.

  • However, we can add a multiple of another row to the [MATH: 2]nd row to make [MATH: a_{22}=0.]

Looking at the first row, we see that [MATH: a_{12}=1.] If we add [MATH: -5] times this entry to [MATH: a_{22},] we will get [MATH: a_{22}=0] as desired. So, the elementary row operation that we need to use is

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1.]

Applying this operation, we obtain the following:

[MATH: A|= [3|1|− 2; − 1|5|6; 0|2|4]R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 5) ⋅ R_{1}; ∼[3|1|− 2; − 1 + (− 5) ⋅ 3|5 + (− 5) ⋅ 1|6 + (− 5) ⋅ (− 2); 0|2|4]; ∼[3|1|− 2; − 16|0|16; 0|2|4]]

Therefore, the desired elemetary row operation is

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1,]

or simply

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 -5 R_1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we are given a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:
[MATH: x_{1} + 3x_{2} − x_{3} = 0; 2x_{1} − x_{2} + 4x_{3} = − 2; 5x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} = 1]

Content:
We can apply some operations to the augmented matrix that do not change the set of solutions for the corresponding system. These operations are called elementary row operations.

Content:
After applying an elementary row operation to the augmented matrix, the new corresponding system will have the same solutions.

Content:
There are three types of elementary row operations:

Content:
- switching any two rows:
[MATH: R_i \leftrightarrow R_j]
- multiplying (each element of) a row by a non-zero number:
[MATH: R_i := k R_i,\qquad k \neq 0]
- adding a multiple of one row to another row:
[MATH: R_j := R_j+k R_i,\qquad j \neq i]

Content:
In the notations above, the "[MATH: :=]" symbol is called the assignment operator. We use this to assign new values to every element of a given row.

Content:
For example, the row operation [MATH: R_1 := 2 R_1] means, "create a new row [MATH: 1] by taking the old row [MATH: 1] and multiplying it by [MATH: 2.]" When we do this, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: M|∼[1|3|− 1|0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]R_{1}:=2R_{1}; ∼[2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 3|2 ⋅ (− 1)|2 ⋅ 0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]; ∼[2|6|− 2|0; 2|− 1|4|− 2; 5|1|1|1]]

Content:
A few final points on notation.

Content:
- We use the similarity symbol ([MATH: \sim]) to indicate when one matrix is transformed into another matrix using elementary row operations.
- The assignment operator [MATH: :=] is sometimes called the "walrus operator" because it looks like a walrus on its side!

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying Row Operations To a Coefficients Matrix

Example Prompt:
Consider the matrix [MATH: A,] given by
[MATH: [1|2|3; 4|2|− 1; 7|12|13]]
What matrix results from carrying out the row operation [MATH: R_2 := R_2 +(- 4) \cdot R_1] on [MATH: A?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2 + (-4) R_1] means that we need to add [MATH: -4] times the first row to the second row.

Carrying out this row operation, we get the following:

[MATH: A|= [1|2|3; 4|2|− 1; 7|12|13]R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 4) ⋅ R_{1}; ∼[1|2|3; 4 + (− 4)(1)|2 + (− 4)(2)|− 1 + (− 4)(3); 7|12|13]; ∼[1|2|3; 0|− 6|− 13; 7|12|13]]

---

Item 5 — Example: Applying Row Operations To an Augmented Matrix

Applying this row operation, we obtain the following:

[MATH: A|= [− 1|5|4|1; 1|0|5|2; 3|7|1|9]R_{1}↔R_{2}; ∼[1|0|5|2; − 1|5|4|1; 3|7|1|9]]

Item 8 — Example: Identifying the Appropriate Row Operation To Transform One Matrix Into Another

Example Prompt:
Which elementary row operation could transform the matrix [MATH: A] into the matrix [MATH: B], where
[MATH: [− 4|− 2|4; 4|1|2; 1|2|3]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the [MATH: 1]st and the [MATH: 3]rd rows are the same in both matrices. The only row that has been changed is the [MATH: 2]nd row.

Now, applying the operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2+1 \cdot R_1,] we get the following:

[MATH: A|= [− 4|− 2|4; 4|1|2; 1|2|3]R_{2}:=R_{2} + 1 ⋅ R_{1}; ∼[− 4|− 2|4; 4 + 1 ⋅ (− 4)|1 + 1 ⋅ (− 2)|2 + 1 ⋅ 4; 1|2|3]; ∼[− 4|− 2|4; 0|− 1|6; 1|2|3]; = B]

Therefore, the transformation could be done by the operation

[MATH: R_2:=R_2+1\cdot R_1]

or simply

[MATH: R_2:=R_2+R_1.]

Item 11 — Example: Identifying the Appropriate Row Operation To Transform a Given Entry to a Desired Value

Example Prompt:
Given that
[MATH: [3|1|− 2; − 1|5|6; 0|2|4]] which elementary row operation could make [MATH: a_{22}=0?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In the given matrix, we have [MATH: a_{22}=5] and we want to perform an elementary row operation that makes [MATH: a_{22}=0.]

- We cannot make [MATH: a_{22}=0] by switching two rows, because there are no rows with [MATH: 0] as the second entry.
- We cannot multiply the second row by [MATH: 0,] because we are only allowed to multiply rows by nonzero constants.
- However, we can add a multiple of another row to the [MATH: 2]nd row to make [MATH: a_{22}=0.]

Looking at the first row, we see that [MATH: a_{12}=1.] If we add [MATH: -5] times this entry to [MATH: a_{22},] we will get [MATH: a_{22}=0] as desired. So, the elementary row operation that we need to use is

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1.]

Applying this operation, we obtain the following:

[MATH: A|= [3|1|− 2; − 1|5|6; 0|2|4]R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 5) ⋅ R_{1}; ∼[3|1|− 2; − 1 + (− 5) ⋅ 3|5 + (− 5) ⋅ 1|6 + (− 5) ⋅ (− 2); 0|2|4]; ∼[3|1|− 2; − 16|0|16; 0|2|4]]

Therefore, the desired elemetary row operation is

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1,]

or simply

[MATH: R_2 := R_2 -5 R_1.]
